What do you use Esperanto for? Who do you speak it with? Are there pockets of Esperanto speakers in certain places?

There are. Basically people all over the world learn it, and so every city or area (regardless of country/region) has a number of people who speak Esperanto. Some places have more and some have less, but it's not really possible for a given place to have zero, even if they're hard to find.

Before the Internet was invented, what they'd do is form local clubs and associations and primarily meet in person. They created what may have been the first global social network in human history. Typically what Esperanto speakers would do for long distances is letter writing, and then travel to meet each other, sometimes very long distances. This could be to attend an international congress, or just privately visiting friends.

Things have changed a bit in the Internet age. Now most Esperanto speakers, especially the younger generations, primarily live online and are often physically absent in meetups, which the older generations seem to prefer. Although even older Esperanto speakers were early adopters of things like e-mail, so many of them are using that at least, or have gotten onto Facebook.

The end result is that because of the Internet, there's always someone to socialize with online, 24/7. It could be chat rooms or other kinds of online groups or communities. Since I learned it in 2015, my single biggest use for it is to socialize, so I've attended a few clubs and conventions and chat with friends online who live in other countries. The whole point is to make friends abroad.

As far as I know there isn't really a fully local Esperanto community like a village or neighborhood where everybody speaks Esperanto. There are families that speak it, usually because the parents met through it and it was their only common language, so they got used to speaking it at home.

You'll usually find more speakers in more largely populated areas like major cities. Some countries seem to have more speakers than other, for example the largest concentration of Esperanto speakers globally seems to live in Europe. It makes sense given the language's history and character, it's rather European, though it also found relative popularity in Asia and the Americas. But the fact is, if you chat with an Esperanto speaker online, you never really know where they're going to be from. Maybe Russia, maybe Brazil, maybe Denmark, maybe America, maybe Japan.

Honestly it's a lot of fun if you're the social type of person or like to travel and see other countries. In some ways it's a little bit like English, which has also become very international, but I think Esperanto gives a different experience, and a good one too. It's so much easier to learn than English, that through Esperanto you get opened up to meeting and getting to know people around the world who may not know English at all, or their Esperanto is much more advanced than their English.
